The issue related to microcode in the Allen-Myland case was whether the defendant’s copying of IBM’s 3090 mainframe computer’s microcode — specifically, copying it into computer memory for analysis and reverse engineering purposes — was permissible under Section 117(1) of the U.S. Copyright Act.

The case centered on the legality of making copies of the microcode (a low-level programming layer that controls the computer’s hardware) to understand how the program operated. The court held that such copying, when done as an essential step in analyzing or reverse engineering the program, was allowed under Section 117(1), which permits copying “as an essential step in the utilization of the computer program in conjunction with a machine.” The court emphasized that the copying was not for the purpose of creating a new program or distributing copies, but for internal analysis and understanding — which aligned with the statutory exception.
